original_question: Does Martin's Axiom imply the existence of a set of reals of cardinality continuum satisfying S1(BOmega,BGamma)?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Problem 4.2 (Examples from CH or MA): Does Martin's Axiom imply the existence of an uncountable set of reals satisfying S1(BΩ, BΓ)? ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the right forcing axiom, the right ambient objects (sets of reals), and the right selection property S1(BΩ, BΓ). It is therefore clearly aimed at Problem 4.2 in the paper. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
missing_details: The paper asks for an uncountable set of reals, not specifically a set of cardinality continuum; cardinality continuum is not the paper's official formulation. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

The question should explicitly quantify over a set X ⊆ R. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

To be stand-alone, S1(A, B) must be defined: for each sequence (𝒰_n) of members of A, one chooses U_n ∈ 𝒰_n so that {U_n : n ∈ N} is a member of B. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

B, BΩ, and BΓ must be defined: they are the collections of countable Borel covers, countable Borel ω-covers, and countable Borel γ-covers of X, respectively. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

The paper's cover convention should be made explicit: covers are nontrivial, meaning X itself is not a member of the cover. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

An ω-cover must be defined: every finite F ⊆ X is contained in some member of the cover. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

A γ-cover must be defined: the cover is infinite and each x ∈ X belongs to all but finitely many members of the cover. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

The paper places this question specifically in the Section 4 discussion of Borel-diagram realizations under CH and MA, after observing that the previously listed constructions carry over to Martin's Axiom except perhaps Setting (n). ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
refined_question: Assume Martin's Axiom. Does there exist an uncountable set of reals X ⊆ R such that for every sequence (𝒰_n)_{n∈N} of countable Borel ω-covers of X, one can choose U_n ∈ 𝒰_n for each n so that {U_n : n ∈ N} is a Borel γ-cover of X? Here each 𝒰_n is a nontrivial cover of X by Borel subsets of X, an ω-cover means that every finite F ⊆ X is contained in some member of 𝒰_n, and a γ-cover means an infinite cover in which each x ∈ X belongs to all but finitely many members. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
justification: This is the nearest official formulation to your draft. Section 4 asks exactly whether Martin's Axiom yields an uncountable set of reals satisfying S1(BΩ, BΓ), and it does so as the remaining MA case after the preceding Borel examples. The notation needed to make the problem self-contained is introduced earlier in the paper: Section 1 defines S1(A, B), while Section 2 defines B, BΩ, and BΓ and gives the relevant cover terminology. The main way your draft departs from the paper is by strengthening uncountable to cardinality continuum. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))
